stemMd: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

options.label: A
options.textMd: To explain how medieval carpenters were able to span wide halls without supporting columns

options.label: B
options.textMd: To argue that the founding charter of the Grimstad hall misidentifies the carpenter who built the original hall

options.label: C
options.textMd: To describe the methods that conservators use to date wooden buildings

options.label: D
options.textMd: To present evidence that the roof credited to Master Håkon was built long after his time by other carpenters

explanationMd:
The purpose of a text is what the whole of it is written to do, so look at where it ends up. The passage opens with a common belief (guidebooks credit the roof to Master Håkon, the carpenter in the 1374 charter), turns on *Yet*, and then gives two independent pieces of evidence against that belief: the beams come from trees felled in the 1560s, and the assembly marks match a workshop active only in that period. The last sentence states the conclusion the evidence supports: the roof is a sixteenth-century replacement.

That pattern (belief, evidence, corrected conclusion) is a text written to challenge an attribution, which is what the choice about presenting evidence that the roof was built long after Master Håkon's time says.

The choice about the charter misidentifying the carpenter is the one to test carefully. The passage never questions the charter; Master Håkon may well have built the *original* roof. What it corrects is the guidebooks' assumption that the roof standing today is that original.

distractorRationale.b: This goes beyond the passage. Nothing suggests the charter is wrong about who built the hall in 1374; the passage argues only that the present roof is a later replacement, so the guidebooks, not the charter, are mistaken.
distractorRationale.a: The unsupported span is mentioned only as the reason visitors admire the roof. The passage never explains how such a span was built.
distractorRationale.c: Tree-ring dating and assembly marks appear as the evidence for Aasen's conclusion, not as the subject of the text. The passage does not describe how either method works.

accessibilityText: Using the passage about the roof of the medieval guild hall at Grimstad and conservator Liv Aasen's dating of its beams, choose the statement that best describes the main purpose of the text.

provenance.notes: Original item. The strongest distractor moves the passage's correction from the guidebooks to the charter, one step beyond what is supported.

review.author: wave7-sat-rw-ideas-craft-author

independentSolve.workingNotes: The passage uses tree-ring dates of the 1560s and later workshop marks to argue that the roof credited to Håkon is a sixteenth-century replacement. That is D. [A second, separate blind solve (blind-reviewer-wave7-sat-rw-run1) reached the same answer: The tree-ring dates (1560s) and the assembly marks of a later workshop are presented as evidence that the roof is a sixteenth-century replacement, not Håkon's. B is wrong because the charter need not be mistaken about the original hall. A and C are side details.]

review.notes: Author's own solve and uniqueness check: the text moves from the guidebooks' attribution through two pieces of dating evidence to the conclusion that the present roof is a 1560s replacement, so its purpose is to challenge the attribution; only the option about presenting evidence the roof was built long after Master Håkon's time states it. The charter option overreaches (the charter is never questioned); the span and dating-method options treat a detail or a tool as the purpose. Re-solved from the stem alone with the same result. Not published: awaiting a blind independent solve by a second party. Options were reordered after review to remove answer-position bias; ids and labels were remapped with the key.
